name: Leaky gut syndrome diet

card.summary: A set of gut-healing eating protocols followed by people who believe a permeable intestinal lining drives skin problems and low energy, with the aim of clearer skin and better vitality.
card.note: Leaky gut syndrome is not a recognised medical diagnosis; restrictive diets can limit nutrient variety.

quick.overview:
Leaky gut diets are elimination-style and supplement-based eating plans promoted for a hypothesised condition in which a permeable gut lining lets substances into the blood and causes inflammation. In appearance circles the hoped-for payoff is clearer skin, less bloating and more energy to train.

Increased intestinal permeability is a measurable phenomenon that researchers study, but leaky gut syndrome as a cause of wide-ranging illness is described by Wikipedia as hypothetical and medically unrecognised. The NHS says there is little evidence for the hypothesis, and advocates are largely nutritionists and alternative practitioners.
quick.how: Protocols typically remove foods such as gluten, sugar or processed items, and add probiotics, herbal remedies or other supplements. Variants include low-FODMAP, low-sugar and antifungal diets. People usually follow them for weeks and track skin and digestion.
quick.risks: Restrictive diets can narrow nutrient intake, and supplements are not adequately tested for this purpose. Anyone with persistent digestive symptoms or skin disease may be advised by clinicians to seek diagnosis for recognised conditions instead of attributing them to leaky gut.

lead: The leaky gut syndrome diet refers to a family of eating plans and supplement stacks built around the idea that a permeable intestinal lining allows gut contents to enter the bloodstream and trigger chronic inflammation. People in wellness and appearance circles follow them to improve skin, reduce bloating and raise energy.[1]

Proponents are mostly nutritionists and alternative medicine practitioners, who link leaky gut to conditions including chronic fatigue, arthritis, migraines and autism. Diets promoted include gluten-free, low-FODMAP, low-sugar and antifungal plans, plus probiotics and herbal supplements.[1]

Wikipedia distinguishes leaky gut syndrome, which it calls hypothetical and medically unrecognised, from increased intestinal permeability, a measurable phenomenon that is a subject of research as a possible target for prevention and therapy. It reports little evidence that the promoted diets help and that none have been adequately tested for this purpose; the NHS and Quackwatch's Stephen Barrett are cited as critical of the concept.[1]

chain: Remove suspected trigger foods and add gut-support products
Claimed clearer skin and more energy
angle.text: Followers adopt gut-healing diets expecting that calmer digestion will show up as clearer skin and steadier energy for training. The link between gut permeability and skin is a claim made by proponents and is not an established clinical pathway.

infobox: Leaky gut syndrome is not a recognised diagnosis

paras: Protocols vary by promoter but share an elimination phase and a repair phase: foods thought to irritate the gut are removed while probiotics, herbal remedies or supplements are added.[1]

Advocates argue that a leaky lining causes systemic inflammation that appears as fatigue, joint pain and skin problems. Skin and energy outcomes are the form most relevant to looks, though Wikipedia's account of claims does not mention them specifically.[1]

Wikipedia reports that evidence for leaky gut syndrome as a cause of disease is weak, that the NHS says there is little evidence for it, and that NICE does not recommend special diets for leaky gut syndrome. A 2016 review by Quigley asked whether it is a concept or a clinical entity.[1] Increased intestinal permeability itself is treated in the literature as a real phenomenon.[1]
No studies found. Studies of intestinal permeability exist, but no trial has shown that a leaky gut diet clears skin or raises energy.[1]
